newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl meets mining union, industry on subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Kohl meets mining union, industry on subsidies.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl and key members of his centre-right coalition government began talks on Thursday with the leader of the German IG Bergbau union aimed at winning support to cut federal subsidies to miners.

The government, under pressure to rein in budget deficits in its bid to qualify for Europe's single currency, hopes to slash the 10 billion marks in aid it pays each year to support more than 90,000 jobs.
Hans Berger, head of IG Bergbau, said ahead of the meeting that he was optimistic, but that the miners would did not see much room to negotiate.

Ahead of the meeting it was expected that the government would for the first time give details of the level of subsidies it would be willing to provide from the year 2005, when the current agreement with the industry expires.

It is widely believed that the government would try to reduce the annual subsidies to around four billion marks, significantly lower than the IG Bergbau union's proposal of 6.5 billion. Berger said the union's proposal would save 12 coalfields and around half the workforce.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt and Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl also attended the meeting.

Afterwards, Kohl was scheduled to meet Gerhard Neipp, chairman of the mining company Ruhrkohle AG and the economics ministers of North Rhine-Westphalia and Saarland states Wolfgang Clement and Christiane Krajewski.
About 100,000 miners and their supporters marched in the Ruhr Valley mining region last month to call for continued subsidies.
German hard coal, which must be dug from deep beneath the earth, costs several times as much as imports, but Bonn has seen fit to maintain at least a token domestic industry.
Berger has said previously that he did not expect the March 6 meeting to product a final decision, but that the situation must be clarified by Easter.
